13 Equivariant \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory (Wednesday, September 22)

The setup: \(G\curvearrowright X\) a topological group acting on a space.

  • Gelfand (30s): replace \(X\) with a topological vector space \(T\), e.g. “generalized functions” on \(X\). This linearises the problem, but is usually something like a infinite dimensional Hilbert space.

  • Harish-Chandra, Vogan: Replace \(T\) with an algebraic object (usually finite-dimensional) and apply \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory. Here \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory simplifies the problem, since all invariants that are additive on exact sequences can be recovered from it.

Classical literature on this is phrased in terms of \(X\) a separated algebraic space, since even nice quotients of varieties are often not again varieties. We’ll assume \(X\) is an algebraic variety, automatically separated, and quasiprojective. This will imply that \(X \subseteq G/P\) embeds into a flag variety, e.g. for \(G = \operatorname{GL}_n\) and \(P\) a parabolic this covers \({\mathbb{P}}^n\). For us, projective will mean that \(X \subseteq G/P\) is closed, which will turn out to admit ample line bundles.

Let \(({-})^ {\operatorname{gp} }\) denote taking the Grothendieck group, then \begin{align*} G_0(G, X) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={\mathsf{Coh}}^G(X)^ {\operatorname{gp} } \\ {\mathsf{K}}_0(G, X) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={ {\mathsf{Bun}}\qty{\operatorname{GL}_r} }^G_{/ {X}} ,\end{align*} i.e. the \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant coherent sheaves and vector bundles respectively.

Note that vector bundles don’t form an abelian category – here instead you take the additive monoid generated by addition of vector bundle. However coherent sheaves do form an abelian category, so this denotes the usual Grothendieck group for abelian categories. Of modern interest: split Grothendieck groups, triangulated, etc.

Here one should think of \({\mathsf{G}}\) as something analogous to Borel-Moore homology, and \({\mathsf{K}}\) is closer to cohomology. Note that in classical settings, one could cap against the fundamental class to get a map between them.

If \(X\) is a smooth \(G{\hbox{-}}\)variety admitting an equivariant ample line bundle, then there is an isomorphism \begin{align*} {\mathsf{K}}_0(G, X) \xrightarrow{?} G_0(G, X) .\end{align*}

This map records how a vector bundle can be regarded as a coherent sheaf! For the rest of today, we’ll assume \(X\) admits a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant ample line bundle and refer to this as condition \(\star\). If this proposition holds, notationally we’ll always write \({\mathsf{K}}^G(X) = {\mathsf{K}}_0(X) = G_0(X)\).

Consider the coherent sheaf \({\mathcal{O}}_x{ {}^{ \scriptscriptstyle\oplus^{n} } }\), which should correspond to the trivial bundle \(X\times {\mathbb{C}}^n \to X\). If \(\xi\) is a vector bundle, then the sheaf of sections is a locally free coherent sheaf.

Every \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant coherent sheaf \({\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(X)\) on \(X\) admits a finite resolution by \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant locally free sheaves of finite type.

  • If \(G =1\), then admitting an ample line bundle as above is equivalent to \(X \subseteq G/P\) being a subvariety. Then \({\mathsf{K}}^G(X) = {\mathsf{K}}(X)\), the algebraic \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory, of \(X\).

  • If \(X = {\operatorname{pt}}\), it is smooth, and \({\mathsf{K}}^G(X) = R(G)\), the representation ring of \(G\). This holds for \(G\) any linear algebraic group.

So this mixes usual \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory and representation theory! It turns out that for \(X={\operatorname{pt}}\), there is an equivalence of categories \({\mathsf{Coh}}^G({\operatorname{pt}}) = { {\mathsf{Bun}}\qty{\operatorname{GL}_r} }^G = {\mathsf{G}{\hbox{-}}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathrm{fd}}\).

If \(X\) is projective and \(G\) is semisimple, then \(\star\) is true. If \(E\to X\) is a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)vector bundle on \(X\) smooth projective, then we’ll write \({\mathsf{K}}^G(X)\) for \({\mathsf{G}}_0(G, X) = {\mathsf{K}}_0(G, X)\).

Every \({\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(X)\) is a quotient of a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant locally free sheaf \({\mathcal{E}}\) of finite type on \(X\).

See proof: Borho, Byrlinksi, MacPherson. Geometric perspective on ring theory?

Let \(G \in {\mathsf{Alg}}{\mathsf{Grp}}\) be linear acting on \(V\in {\mathsf{{\mathbb{C}}}{\hbox{-}}\mathsf{Mod}}\) possibly infinite dimensional. This is common, e.g. when \(G\) consists of regular functions. This is infinite dimensional, but not so bad – it’s not quite as big as a Hilbert space. We’ll say the action is algebraic if it acts locally finitely: the \(G{\hbox{-}}\)orbit of any vector should be a finite dimensional subspace. Consider \(\mathop{\mathrm{Maps}}(G, M) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{{\mathsf{Set}}}(G, M) = \left\{{ f:G\to M}\right\}\) with no conditions at all on the functions. There is a subspace of “regular functions with coefficients in \(M\),” using the following well-defined map: \begin{align*} {\mathbb{C}}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{C}}M &\to \mathop{\mathrm{Maps}}(G, M) \\ \sum f_i \otimes m_i &\mapsto \sum f(g_i) m_i ,\end{align*} using that the \(f(g_i)\) are scalars in \(M\).

For a fixed \(m\), there is a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)action \(g\mapsto gm\), and so letting \(m\) vary yields a map \(M \xrightarrow{a_M} \mathop{\mathrm{Maps}}(G, M)\).

\(G\) acts algebraically on \(M\) iff \(\operatorname{im}a_m \subseteq {\mathbb{C}}[G]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}M\).

If the action is algebraic, take \(G_m \subseteq V \subseteq M\) with \(V\) a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)stable finite dimensional subspace. Expanding in a basis and writing \(g\mapsto gm\) in this basis yields the \(f_i\), which are regular.

If \({\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(X)\), then \({{\Gamma}\qty{X; {\mathcal{F}}} }\) has the natural structure of an algebraic \(G{\hbox{-}}\)module.

14 Localization in Equivariant \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory (Friday, September 24)

14.1 Localization Theorems

Reference: Thomason.

Suppose \(A\in {\mathsf{Ab}}{\mathsf{Alg}}{\mathsf{Grp}}\) is reductive, and \(X \subseteq G/P\) is contained in a flag variety (so \(X\) is quasiprojective). Fix \(a\in A\), and consider the fixed point set \(X^a\) and the inclusion \(\iota: X^a \xrightarrow{\subseteq } X\). We’ll say the localization theorem holds for \(X\) if the following induced hom is an isomorphism: \begin{align*} i_*: {\mathsf{K}}^A(X^a) \left[ { \scriptstyle { {{\mathfrak{m}}_a}^{-1}} } \right] \to {\mathsf{K}}^A(X) \left[ { \scriptstyle { {{\mathfrak{m}}_a}^{-1}} } \right] .\end{align*}

Thomason shows that this is true in this situation. Recall that we identified \(R(A) = {\mathsf{K}}^A({\operatorname{pt}})\). Taking the trace of a representation yields a map \(R(A) \hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}[A]\), the ring of regular functions. For varieties, we can obtain \({\mathcal{O}}_{X, x}\) by localizing rings at their maximal ideals, thinking of these as functions on \(X\). Let \begin{align*} R_a &\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= R(A) \left[ { \scriptstyle { { \qty{ R(A)\setminus{\mathfrak{m}}_a} }^{-1}} } \right] \\ M_a &\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= R(A) \otimes_{R(A)} M .\end{align*}

14.2 Proper Pushforward

We’ll need proper maps for the ever-popular decomposition theorem. However, almost every scheme we use in this class will be reduced, although one does rarely have to worry about this.

Pullbacks are universal with respect to the following squares, and have a concrete description for us:

Link to Diagram

The diagonal is the unique morphism \(\Delta: X\to X{ \underset{\scriptscriptstyle {Y} }{\times} } X\) whose compositions with projections are the identity:

Link to Diagram

A morphism is separated if the diagonal is a closed embedding.

A morphism \(f:X\to Y\) is universally closed if for any \(g:Z\to Y\), the base change \(f': X{ \underset{\scriptscriptstyle {Y} }{\times} } Z\to Z\) is a closed morphism. This replaces the notion of “\(K\) compact \(\implies f^{-1}(K)\) compact” for analytic varieties.

A morphism \(f\) is proper if \(f\) is separated, finite type, and universally closed.

  • Closed embeddings are proper, and open maps are usually not.
  • If \(f\) is proper, its base change \(f'\) is always proper.
  • Compositions of proper morphisms are again proper.
  • Any morphism between projective varieties is proper.

Let \(f:X\to Y\) be proper and \({\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Coh}}(X)\). Note that \({{\Gamma}\qty{X, {-}} }\) is exact and \({\mathsf{Coh}}(X)\) is abelian, so we can take its derived functor. Let \(f_*: {\mathsf{Sh}}_{/ {X}} \to {\mathsf{Sh}}_{/ {Y}}\), then e.g.  \begin{align*} {\mathbb{R}}^i f_* {\mathcal{F}}(U) = H^i(f^{-1}(U); {\mathcal{F}}) .\end{align*}

This satisfies several properties:

  1. \({\mathbb{R}}^if_*: {\mathsf{Coh}}(X) \to {\mathsf{Coh}}(Y)\) is a covariant functor. Without properness, one can just replace \({\mathsf{Coh}}\) with \({\mathsf{QCoh}}\).

  2. \({\mathbb{R}}^0 f_* = f_*\)

  3. A SES \(0\to{\mathcal{F}}_1\to{\mathcal{F}}_2\to{\mathcal{F}}_3\to 0\) induces a LES.

If \(f:X\to Y\) is a proper projective morphism, then \({\mathbb{R}}^{i>d} f_* {\mathcal{F}}= 0\) for \(d\) defined as the maximum dimension of the fiber, \(d\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=\max_{y\in Y} \dim f^{-1}(y)\).

Let \(X, Y\) be arbitrary quasiprojective varieties and \(f:X\to Y\) be proper and \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant. Then there is a natural direct image morphism \(f_*: {\mathsf{K}}^G(X) \to {\mathsf{K}}_G(Y)\).

We define it as follows: note that a map such as \(f_*([{\mathcal{F}}]) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=[f_* {\mathcal{F}}]\) won’t necessarily be well-defined, since SESs are additive in the Grothendieck group. For \({\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(X)\), then it turns out that \({\mathbb{R}}f_* {\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(Y)\) and the higher direct images vanish in large enough degree. We then define \begin{align*} f_*: {\mathsf{K}}^G(X) &\to {\mathsf{K}}_G(Y) \\ [{\mathcal{F}}] &\mapsto \sum (-1)^i [{\mathbb{R}}^i f_* {\mathcal{F}}] .\end{align*}

Let \(G\) be connected reductive with \(A \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= T\) a maximal torus, which is abelian reductive. Then take \(a\in A\) a regular element, so \(X^a = X^T\). In our case, \(X^T = W_Y'\), and \(X = G/P_Y\). Then \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory is concentrated on the fixed locus: \begin{align*} i_* {\mathsf{K}}^T(X^T) \left[ { \scriptstyle { {{\mathfrak{m}}_a}^{-1}} } \right] { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}^T(X) \left[ { \scriptstyle { {{\mathfrak{m}}_a}^{-1}} } \right] .\end{align*}

15 Line Bundles on \({\mathcal{X}}^Y\) (Monday, September 27)

Notation: \({\mathcal{X}}\) will denote a Kac-Moody flag variety, and \(X\) a usual flag variety. For any \(\lambda \in D_Y^0\), define the algebraic line bundle \({\mathcal{L}}(-\lambda) \to {\mathcal{X}}^Y\) to be the pullback of the tautological bundle on \({\mathbb{P}}(L^{\max}(\lambda))\) via the morphism \(\iota_\lambda: {\mathcal{X}}^Y \to {\mathbb{P}}(L^{\max} (\lambda))\). Recall that we defined \(Y{\hbox{-}}\)regular weights to get an embedding into a flag variety.

Let \(X\) be a finite dimensional variety, then a vector bundle on \(X\) is a map \({\mathcal{E}}\xrightarrow{\pi} X\) with each fiber a \({\mathbb{C}}{\hbox{-}}\)module and for all \(x\in X\) there exists an open \(U \subseteq X\) and a homeomorphism \(\phi: U \times {\mathbb{C}}^n \to \pi^{-1}(U)\) over \(U\), so the following diagram commutes:

Link to Diagram

We refer to \(\phi\) as a trivialization. Writing \(U_{12} \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= U_1 \cap U_2\), given trivializations over \(U_i\) we require that the trivializations on \(U_{12}\) are related by an element \(T_{12} \in \operatorname{GL}_n\), and the induced map \(U_{12} \times {\mathbb{C}}^n{\circlearrowleft}\) are essentially given by matrices with entries given by functions on \(U_{12}\) The key is that these satisfy the cocycle condition: \begin{align*} T_{kj}\mathrel{\Big|}_{U_{ijjk}} T_{ji} \mathrel{\Big|}_{U_{ijk}} = T_{ki}\mathrel{\Big|}_{U_{ijk}} .\end{align*}

Given a vector bundle, set \({\mathcal{F}}\) to be the sheaf of sections of \(\pi: {\mathcal{E}}\to X\). If for example \(U \subseteq X\) is trivializable, then \({{\Gamma}\qty{U, {\mathcal{F}}} }\) are \(n{\hbox{-}}\)tuples of functions \(U\to {\mathbb{C}}\), so \({ \left.{{{\mathcal{F}}}} \right|_{{U}} }\cong {\mathcal{O}}_U{ {}^{ \scriptscriptstyle\oplus^{n} } }\), making it locally free.

Given a vector bundle, set \({\mathcal{F}}\) to be the sheaf of sections of \(\pi: {\mathcal{E}}\to X\). Then

  1. If \({\mathcal{F}}\) is locally free, then \(\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{{\mathsf{Sh}}_{/ {X}} }({\mathcal{F}}, {\mathcal{O}}_X) \in {\mathsf{Sh}}_{/ {X}}\) is locally free.
  2. If \(n=1\), then \({\mathcal{F}}\otimes{\mathcal{F}} {}^{ \vee }\cong {\mathcal{O}}_X\), making it an invertible sheaf under the monoidal tensor product.
  3. Pullbacks of locally free sheaves are again locally free:

where we equivalently write \(f^* {\mathcal{F}}\).

How to think about a flag variety: given \(w\in W_Y'\) and \(U_W \subseteq X^Y\), so \(U^- \subseteq G/P\). Then \(\left\{{U_w}\right\}_{w\in W_Y'} \rightrightarrows X^Y\) is an open cover with \(U_w \cong {\mathbb{C}}^{\ell(w_0')}\) with \(w_0\) the longest element and \(w_0'\) is a minimal coset representative. If \(v\in U_w \iff v=w\) for any \(T{\hbox{-}}\)fixed point \(v\), so there’s only one such fixed point in every open. We have elements \(wP/p \in X^Y\), so

For \(G \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={\operatorname{SL}}_{n+1}\), we have \(Y = \left\{{2,\cdots, n}\right\}, W = S_{n+1} = \left\{{(w_0 \cdots w_n)}\right\}\) and the minimal length representatives have increasing coordinates, so we get \begin{align*} W_Y' = \left\{{(0 \mathrel{\Big|}1,2\cdots, n), (1 \mathrel{\Big|}0, 2, \cdots, n), \cdots , (n\mathrel{\Big|}0,1\cdots, n-1)}\right\} .\end{align*} For every \(i\in W_Y' = \left\{{0, \cdots, n}\right\}\), we have \(U_i \subseteq X^Y \subseteq G/P_Y\). So we can take \(U_i \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=\left\{{ {\left[ {x_0,\cdots, x_n} \right]} {~\mathrel{\Big\vert}~}x_i\neq 0 }\right\} \subseteq {\mathbb{C}}^n\), which is dimension \(n\) since the longest element is \((n \mathrel{\Big|}0,1,\cdots, n-1)\).

Let \(k\in {\mathbb{Z}}\), we’ll define \({\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^n}(k)\), a line bundle on \({\mathbb{P}}^n\). Taking \(n=1\) to get \({\operatorname{SL}}_2\) and \({\mathbb{P}}^1\) above, we have \(W_Y' = \left\{{0, 1}\right\}\) and \({\mathbb{C}}= U_1 = \operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{C}}[x_{0/1}]\) and \(U_0 = \operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{C}}[x_{0/1}]\), then on their intersection we have \(x_{0/1} = x_{1/0}^{-1}\). So transitioning \(U_0\to U_1\) is given by \(x_{0/1}^k = x_{1/0}^{-k}\), and \(U_1\to U_0\) by \(x_{1/0}^k = x_{0/1}^{-k}\), which defines a line bundle denoted \({\mathcal{E}}\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={\mathcal{O}}(k)\). What are the global sections \({{\Gamma}\qty{{\mathbb{P}}^1; {\mathcal{O}}(k)} }\)? This requires \(f(x_{0/1}^{-1}) x_{0/1}^k = g(x_{0/1})\), so the global sections are \({\mathbb{C}}[x,y]_{k}\) the homogeneous polynomials of degree \(k\). One can check that \(\dim {{\Gamma}\qty{{\mathbb{P}}^n; {\mathcal{O}}(k)} } = {n+k \choose k}\).

Next time: we’ll try to match these up with line bundles of the form \(G \overset{\scriptscriptstyle {P} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_\lambda\).

18 Cohomology of Certain Line Bundles \(Z_w\) (Monday, October 04)

Some references:

  • Fulton, Intersection Theory. Similar difficulty to Hartshorne if you’re going through it yourself!

    • See Young Tableaux books.

  • Eisenbud-Harris, 3264 and All That. A more Vakil-style approach.

The Chow group of \(X\in{\mathsf{Var}}_{/ {k}}\) is the quotient \(A_*(X) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= Z(X)/ \operatorname{Rat}(X)\), where \(Z(X) = {\mathbb{Z}}[{\mathrm{Sub}}(X)]\), the free \({\mathbb{Z}}{\hbox{-}}\)module on subvarieties of \(X\). The group \(Z(X)\) are algebraic cycle, and we mod out by rational equivalence.

If \(G\curvearrowright X\), then \(Y\sim gY\in A_*(X)\), and something similar happens for many algebraic group actions. Another example is that in \({\mathbb{P}}^1\), \(x \sim x'\) for all points \(x,x'\) since \({\operatorname{PSL}}_2\curvearrowright{\mathbb{P}}^1\).

Note that there is also an equivariant Chow group/ring. In general, \(A_*(X)\) is difficult/impossible to compute (according to Harris) unless there is an affine stratification. In these cases, it coincides with Borel-Moore homology.

If \(X\) is smooth, then \(A^*(X)\) forms a ring, where the grading is given by codimension of subvarieties. Thus there is a multiplication \([A] \cdot [B] = [A \cap B]\) when \(A\pitchfork B\) generically. Here transversality refers to an open condition on tangent spaces.

We have three ways of thinking about line bundles:

  • Local trivializations
  • Algebraic morphisms with 1-dimensional fibers
  • Invertible sheaves

Now we’ll add a fourth in terms of divisors. Define:

  • \(A_{n-1}(X)\in {\mathsf{Grp}}\), Weil divisors
  • \({\operatorname{Pic}}(X) \in {\mathsf{Grp}}\), the group of isomorphism classes of algebraic line bundles on \(X\) where \([L_1] \cdot [L_2] \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=[L_1 \oplus L_2]\).

Taking the Chern class yields a group morphism \(c_1: {\operatorname{Pic}}(X) \to A_{n-1}(X)\). If the line bundle is generated by global sections, take the zero section of the global section. If \(X\) is smooth, \(c_1\) is an isomorphism, and we write \(c_1({\mathcal{O}}_X(Y)) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=[Y]\in A_{n-1}(X)\). Note that this is slightly different to the ideal sheaf definition in Vakil.

See relation to Schubert varieties and Grassmannians in the referenced books. Bott-Samelson-Demazure and flag varieties will be smooth, although we’ll have to be careful for Schubert varieties.

Define the length of a word \(w\in W\) to be the number of simple reflections, regardless of whether or not \(w\) is reduced. Let \(n\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=\ell(w)\), then there is a formula for the canonical bundle \(K_{Z_w}\) of any Bott-Samelson-Demazure variety \(Z_w\) (even Kac-Moody types): \begin{align*} {\mathcal{L}}_w(-\rho) \otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{Z_w}( - \sum_{q=1}^n Z_{w(q)} ) .\end{align*}

Here \(\rho\in {\mathfrak{h}} {}^{ \vee }_{\mathbb{Z}}\) (e.g. characters of the torus in the semisimple simply connected case) is any element satisfying \(\rho( \alpha_i {}^{ \vee }) = 1\) for all \(1\leq i \leq \ell\). Recall that \begin{align*} Z_w = P_{i_1}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} \cdots \overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} P_{i_n} / B = \left\{{ {\left[ {p_1, \cdots, p_n B/B } \right]}}\right\} ,\end{align*} and \(Z_w(q)\) means deleting the \(q\)th factor, so \(Z_w(q) = \left\{{{\left[ {p_1,\cdots, 1,\cdots, p_nB/B} \right]}}\right\}\) has the \(q\)th coordinate set to 1. Note that there is a quotient map \(Z_w \to Z_{w(n)}\), which has a section, and we can use this to induct.

Consider \(G\) connected and reductive and let \(X=G/B\) be the flag variety, which is smooth. Then for \(\lambda \in X(T)\) corresponds to the algebraic line bundle \({\mathcal{L}}^{\emptyset}( \lambda) = G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{ - \lambda}\). This yields a function \(X(T) \to {\operatorname{Pic}}(X) \xrightarrow{c_1} A_{n-1}(X)\) given by forgetting the \(G{\hbox{-}}\)action. This is a group morphism, where adding characters maps to tensoring bundles.

Note that for \(T = {\mathbb{C}}^{\times}\), we have \begin{align*} X(T) = \mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{{\mathsf{Alg}}{\mathsf{Grp}}}({\mathbb{C}}^{\times}, {\mathbb{C}}^{\times})= \left\{{z \mapsto z^k {~\mathrel{\Big\vert}~}k\in {\mathbb{Z}}}\right\} { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}_{{\mathsf{Ab}}{\mathsf{Grp}}} {\mathbb{Z}} ,\end{align*} where negatives are permitted since \(0\not\in {\mathbb{C}}^{\times}\). More generally, \(X(T) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}_{{\mathsf{Ab}}{\mathsf{Grp}}} {\mathbb{Z}}^n\) for \(n=\operatorname{rank}T\), where \({\left[ {{ {t}_1, {t}_2, \cdots, {t}_{n}}} \right]} \xrightarrow{\lambda} \lambda_1^{k_1}\cdots \lambda_n^{k_n}\). Since we have an affine stratification by Schubert cells, we can write \(A_*(X) = \bigoplus_{w\in W} [X_w]\), and in fact \(A_k(X) = \bigoplus _{\ell(w) = k} [X_w]\). Considering the lattice for \(W\), there are \(\ell\) dimension 1 Schubert cells, and identifying them as CW cells and applying Poincare duality, there are \(\ell\) codimension 1 cells:

Link to Diagram

It turns out that the map is given as follows: \begin{align*} {\mathbb{Z}}^n \cong X(T) &\longrightarrow A_{n-1}(X) \cong {\mathbb{Z}}^\ell \\ \lambda&\mapsto \sum_{i=1}^\ell {\left\langle {\lambda},~{ \alpha_i {}^{ \vee }} \right\rangle}[X_{w_0 s_i}] && n\geq \ell .\end{align*}

For \(G = {\operatorname{SL}}_2, {\mathcal{L}}( \lambda_k) = {\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^1}(k)\) and \(X(T) \cong {\mathbb{Z}}\). Recall that \({{\Gamma}\qty{{\mathbb{P}}^1, {\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^1}(k)} } = {\mathbb{C}}[x, y]_k\) are homogeneous polynomials of degree \(k\) when \(k\geq 0\), otherwise there are no global sections. For example, \({\mathbb{C}}[x, y]_2 = \left\langle{x^2, xy, y^2}\right\rangle\) is dimension \(3 = 2 + 1\). All points are rationally equivalent, so we can take the basepoint \(B/B\), and so the map will need to track the multiplicity of points. The composition is given by the following:

Link to Diagram

The cotangent bundle of \(X\) is given by \(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {P} }{\times} u = T {}^{ \vee }G/P\) where \(P = LU\). The canonical bundle is the top wedge power, and here we get \(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathfrak{n}}= G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_2 = {\mathcal{L}}(-2)\), noting that the canonical is equal to the cotangent bundle here, and we’ve identified which equivariant bundle this is.

19 Friday, October 08

Continuing some stuff from Kumar Ch. 8: the goal is to understand the Demazure and Weyl-Kac character formulas. Open question: how can one compute the singular locus of a given Schubert variety? This is surprisingly a hot topic this semester, c/o multiple Arxiv papers that have come out over the past few months.

Our first goal: showing \(X_w^Y\) is normal. Note that most varieties in representation theory are not normal, and this complicates things significantly, so normality is a great condition here.

Recall that for \(X\in {\mathsf{Var}}\), the stalks \({\mathcal{O}}_{X, x}\) are local rings, and the cotangent space at \(x\) is defined as \({\mathfrak{m}}_x/{\mathfrak{m}}_x^2\).

Cohomology vanishing: some of the hardest and most important results in this area!

Let \(w = (s_{i_1} \cdots, s_{i_n}) \in W\) be a word and consider \(j, k\) such that \(1\leq j\leq k\leq n\). Suppose that the subword \(v = (s_{i_j} \cdots, s_{i_k})\) is reduced. Considering the associated BSDH-varieties, we have a subvariety \begin{align*} Z_v \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= P_{i_j}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} \cdots P_{i_k}/B \hookrightarrow Z_w \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= P_{i_1}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} \cdots P_{i_n}/B .\end{align*} Recall that \({\mathcal{L}}^Y(\lambda) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {P_Y} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{- \lambda}\), and \begin{align*} {\mathcal{L}}_w( \lambda) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= P_{i_1}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} \cdots \overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} P_{i_n} {\mathbb{C}}_{- \lambda} = f^* {\mathcal{L}}^Y( \lambda) ,\end{align*} and we write \(w(n)\) for \(w\) with the \(n\)th letter omitted. Moreover codimension 1 subvarieties correspond to line bundles under the Chern class isomorphism. Then for any integral dominant \(\lambda \in D_{\mathbb{Z}}\), there are 3 vanishing formulas:

  1. \begin{align*} H^{\geq 1 } \qty{ Z_w; {\mathcal{L}}_w( \lambda) \otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{Z_w}(- \sum_{q=0}^k Z_{w(q)} ) } &= 0 .\end{align*}

  2. \begin{align*} H^{\geq 1} \qty{Z_w; {\mathcal{L}}_w( \lambda) } &= 0 .\end{align*}

  3. If \(k<n\) and \(v' \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=(s_{i_k} \cdots, s_{i_k} s_{i_{k+1}})\) is not reduced, then

\begin{align*} H^{\geq 0 } \qty{ Z_w; {\mathcal{L}}_w( \lambda) \otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{Z_v}(- \sum_{q=j}^k Z_{w(q)} ) } &= 0 \\ .\end{align*}

We’ll often use Serre duality in the following form: given a set of nice assumptions, there is a perfect pairing \begin{align*} H^i(X; {\mathcal{F}}) \times H^{n-i}(X; K_X \otimes{\mathcal{F}} {}^{ \vee }) \to {\mathbb{C}} ,\end{align*} where \({\mathcal{F}} {}^{ \vee }\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{{\mathcal{O}}_X}({\mathcal{F}}, {\mathcal{O}}_X)\) and \(K_X\) is the dualizing sheaf. Note that if \(X\) is smooth and projective, one can take \(K_X\) to be the canonical sheaf.

For any finite-dimensional representation \(M\) of \(B{ {}^{ \scriptscriptstyle\times^{n} } }\), there is a functorial assignment a \(P_{i_1}{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant algebraic vector bundle \({\mathcal{L}}_w(M) \to Z_w\) on the BSDH variety. which is an exact functor on \({\mathsf{B{ {}^{ \scriptscriptstyle\times^{n} } }}{\hbox{-}}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\dim < \infty}\), given by \begin{align*} {\mathcal{L}}_w( - \lambda ) = {\mathcal{L}}_w( {\mathbb{C}}_{ \lambda}) .\end{align*} This is induced by \(B{ {}^{ \scriptscriptstyle\times^{n} } } \xrightarrow{{\operatorname{pr}}_n} B \to {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda}\).

Using this formula, \begin{align*} {\mathcal{L}}(\lambda) {}^{ \vee }= {\mathcal{L}}( {\mathbb{C}}_{- \lambda}) {}^{ \vee }= {\mathcal{L}}({\mathbb{C}}_{- \lambda} {}^{ \vee }) ,\end{align*} where given \(V_{ \lambda}\) a highest weight representation of \(G\) (connected reductive finite type), we have \(V_{ \lambda} {}^{ \vee }= V_{-w_0 \lambda}\). Let \(X\in {\mathsf{Var}}_{/ {k}}\) be irreducible, then \(X\) is normal at \(x\in X\) iff \({\mathfrak{m}}_x \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={\mathcal{O}}_{X, x}\) is integrally closed in its field of fractions \(\operatorname{ff}({\mathfrak{m}}_x)\).

Note that there are implications smooth \(\implies\) factorial \(\implies\) normal in \({\mathsf{Var}}_{/ {k}}\). We write \(\Sigma(X) \subseteq X\) to be the singular locus, and if \(X\) is normal then \(\operatorname{codim}_X \Sigma(X) \leq 2\).

Let \(f(x,y,z) = x^2-zy^2\) and consider \(X \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= V(f) \subseteq {\mathbb{A}}^3_{/ {{\mathbb{C}}}} \in {\mathsf{Aff}}{\mathsf{Var}}_{/ {{\mathbb{C}}}}\). Checking normality for affine varieties just amounts to checking on regular functions, so \(X\) is normal iff \({\mathbb{C}}[X] \hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}(X)\) is integrally closed. One direction involves checking that localizations are integrally closed, which is an easy exercise in commutative algebra, while the other direction is harder. Consider \(X({\mathbb{R}})\):

The claim is that \(X\) is not normal. Setting \(\xi = x/y\) is not a regular function on \(X\) since \(y\) vanishes at some points of \(X\), but \(\xi^2 = x^2/y^2 = z \in {\mathbb{C}}[X]\) is regular.

Motivating question: normality is a local condition, so where can \(X\) be non-normal? There is a process of normalization which associates to \(X\) a unique normal variety \(\tilde X\) with a unique finite birational morphism \(\nu: \tilde X\to X\). Here finite means points have finite fibers and the map is proper.

Some properties: - \(\nu\) is unique.

  • \(\tilde X \xrightarrow{\nu} X\) satisfies a universal property: For \(X\to Y\) for any \(Y\) normal, then there exists a unique lift

Link to Diagram

See also Stein factorization for proper morphisms.

  • If \(f:X\to Y\) is a birational projective morphism between irreducible varieties and \(Y\) is normal, then \(f_* {\mathcal{O}}_X = {\mathcal{O}}_Y\).

    See also Zariski’s main theorem.

Let \(X\) be the umbrella from above. Consider \(\nu(u, v) = {\left[ {uv, v, v^2} \right]}\), so \({\mathbb{A}}^2_{/ {{\mathbb{C}}}} \xrightarrow{\nu} X \subseteq {\mathbb{A}}^3_{/ {{\mathbb{C}}}}\), and let \(f(x,y,z) = x^2 - zy^2\), so \(f(uv, v, v^w) = (uv)^2 - u^2v^2 = 0\) is a regular function on \(X\). One can check that \(\Im(\nu) \subseteq X\) so this is surjective, and the conclusion is that \(X\) is irreducible with 2-dimensional fibers. Consider the fibers of \(\nu\):

  1. \(\mathbf{x} = 0\) yields \(\nu^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\{{ {\left[ {u, v} \right]} \in {\mathbb{A}}^2 {~\mathrel{\Big\vert}~}{\left[ {uv, v, u^2} \right]} = \mathbf{0}}\right\} = {\operatorname{pt}}\).
  2. \(\mathbf{x} = {\left[ {0,0, z} \right]}\) with \(z\neq 0\) yields \(\nu^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\{{{\left[ {uv, v, u^2} \right]} = {\left[ {0,0,z} \right]}}\right\} = \left\{{p_1, p_2}\right\}\) which have nonzero 2nd coordinates, by choosing a square root of \(u\).
  3. \(\mathbf{x} = {\left[ {x,y,z} \right]}\) with \(x\neq 0\) yields \(\nu^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\{{{\left[ {uv, v, u^2} \right]} = {\left[ {x,y,z} \right]}}\right\}\). This forces \(v=y\), and \(x = uv= uy\) which is nonzero and can be solved for \(u\), so we again get a single point \(\nu^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = {\operatorname{pt}}\).

Note that just considering the real points misses the entire \(-z\) axis. This can be analyzed by regarding \(u,v\in {\mathbb{C}}\) as a pair of points in the same plane; then if \(u=v=0\) corresponds to (1), \(v=0\) with \(u\) varying yields (2) (and two-point fibers), and moving \(v\) from 0 yields (3). Here \(X\) is normal at the points in (1), but not normal in (2) and (3).

Moral: we can study singularities by looking at fibers.

Vogan: there are more statements in representation theory that say “if normal” than there are that say “then normal.”

Recall that the normalization \(\tilde Y \xrightarrow{\nu} Y\) satisfies a universal property with respect to maps from normal varieties. Using functoriality, we have \begin{align*} f_* {\mathcal{O}}_X &= (\nu \circ \tilde f)_* {\mathcal{O}}_X \\ &= \nu_* (\tilde f_* {\mathcal{O}}_X) \\ &= \nu_* {\mathcal{O}}_{\tilde Y} &&\text{Zariski's Main Theorem, forward direction}\\ &= {\mathcal{O}}_Y &&\text{by assumption} .\end{align*} Use that \(\tilde f\) is birational and proper, where properness can be shown by exhibiting it as the pullback of a proper morphism. Using that \(Y\) is normal iff every open affine \(U \subseteq Y\) is normal, we have \begin{align*} {\mathcal{O}}_Y(U) = (\nu_* {\mathcal{O}}_{\tilde Y})(U) = {\mathcal{O}}_{\tilde Y}(\nu^{-1}(U)) .\end{align*}

23.1 Statements in Equivariant \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory

See Chris-Ginzburg

On flat pullback: for \(f:X\to Y\) a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant morphism of \(G{\hbox{-}}\)spaces, if \(f\) is flat (so tensor-exact) then there is a morphism of \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theories: \begin{align*} f^*: K_i^G(Y) \to K_i^G(X) \end{align*} induced by an exact pullback functor \begin{align*} f^*: {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(Y) & \to {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(X) \\ {\mathcal{F}}&\mapsto f^* {\mathcal{F}}= {\mathcal{O}}_{X} \otimes_{f^{-1}{\mathcal{O}}_Y} f^{-1}{\mathcal{F}} .\end{align*}

Flat implies sameness among fibers in a bundle.

23.2.2 Restriction/Induction

For \(H \leq G\) a closed subgroup and \(X\) an \(H{\hbox{-}}\)space, then \(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {H} }{\times} X\) is always an algebraic variety. E.g. for \(X = {\operatorname{pt}}\), \(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {H} }{\times} {\operatorname{pt}}= G/H\). Note that there is a projection \(G\times X \to G\) where \(H\) acts diagonally on the left and \(G\) is an \(H{\hbox{-}}\)space, and this map is \(H{\hbox{-}}\) equivariant, so there is an induced map \(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {H} }{\times}X\to G/H\). What’s hard is showing there are varieties. This is flat with fiber \(X\) since it’s a fiber bundle in our case.

For \({\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Sh}}^G(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {H} }{\times} X)\) a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant sheaf,

There is a functor \begin{align*} \operatorname{Ind}_H^G: {\mathsf{Coh}}^H(X) &\to {\mathsf{Coh}}^G(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {H} }{\times} X) .\end{align*}

For \(p:G\times X\to X\) and \({\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Sh}}^H(X)\) an \(H{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant sheaf, we can use a diagonal action to obtain \(p^* {\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Sh}}^H(X)\) and write \begin{align*} \operatorname{Ind}_H^G = p^* {\mathcal{F}}\in {\mathsf{Coh}}(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {H} }{\times} X) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{Coh}}^H(G\times H) .\end{align*} This defines a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant structure on \(p^* {\mathcal{F}}\).

Any linear \(G\in {\mathsf{Alg}}{\mathsf{Grp}}\) can be written as \(G\cong R\rtimes U\) where \(R\) is reductive and \(U\) is unipotent.

For any \(X\in {G}{\hbox{-}}{\mathsf{Spaces}}\), \begin{align*} K^G(X) \cong K^R(X) .\end{align*}

Only the reductive groups matter for equivariant \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory.

Define the morphism \(K^G(X)\to K^R(X)\) by forgetting the action away from the subgroup \(R \leq X\): \begin{align*} G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {R} }{\times} X &\xrightarrow{\phi} G/R \times X \\ [g, x] &\mapsto (gR/R, gx) .\end{align*} This induces \begin{align*} {\mathsf{K}}^R(X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Ind}_R^G} {\mathsf{K}}^G(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {R} }{\times} X) \underset{{\mathsf{K}}\phi }{{ { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}} {\mathsf{K}}^G(G/R \times X) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}^G(X) ,\end{align*} using that \(G/R\) is affine.

More generally, for \(E\to X\in { {\mathsf{Bun}}\qty{\operatorname{GL}_r} }^G\), the fibers are contractible and thus \({\mathsf{K}}^G(E) \cong {\mathsf{K}}^G(X)\). See the Thom isomorphism, referenced in Borbo-Brylinksi-MacPherson.

Let \(\pi: G/B \to G/P\) where \(P\) corresponds to the simple reflection \(s\), so \(P\) is the smallest parabolic not equal to the Borel. Then

  • Any map between projective varieties is proper, so \(\pi\) is proper and the fibers are copies of \({\mathbb{P}}^1\), i.e. \(\pi^{-1}(gP/P) = gP/B \cong {\mathbb{P}}^1\).
  • \(\pi\) is smooth in the sense of Hartshorne, i.e. so smooth fibers that are “the same.”

Consequently, \(\pi\) is flat, and \(G/B \cong G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {P} }{\times} P/B \to G/P\) with \(G/B\to G/P\) flat. We can push forward along proper maps and pull back along flat maps, so here we can do both. So define a map \begin{align*} D: {\mathsf{K}}^G(G/B) &\to {\mathsf{K}}^G(G/B) \\ [{\mathcal{F}}] &\mapsto \pi^*\pi_*[{\mathcal{F}}] .\end{align*} Note that this factors as \({\mathsf{K}}^G(G/B) \xrightarrow{\pi_*} {\mathsf{K}}^G(G/P) \xrightarrow{\pi_*} {\mathsf{K}}^G(G/B)\). The question is now what \(\pi^* \pi_* [{\mathcal{F}}]\) actually is.

The idea: we can recover representations as \({\mathsf{K}}^G({\operatorname{pt}})\), which is hard, so we apply these \(D\) operators to larger parabolics to get to a point one step at a time.

We have \(A(T) = {\mathbb{Z}}[X(T)] \cong {\mathsf{K}}^T({\operatorname{pt}})\) for \(A(T)\) representations of the torus. On notation: write \(\lambda \in X(T)\) as \(e^{\lambda} \in A(T)\). Note that \({\mathsf{K}}^P(P/B) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}^P(P\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\operatorname{pt}}) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}^B({\operatorname{pt}})\) and \(A(T) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}^T({\operatorname{pt}})\), so writing \(B = T\rtimes U\), there is an isomorphism \begin{align*} A(T) &{ { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}^P(P/B) \\ C^{\lambda} &\mapsto [P\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{ \lambda}] \mapsto [G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda}] ,\end{align*} which is a composition \(\operatorname{Ind}_P^B \circ \operatorname{Ind}_T^P\). One can regard this as a line bundle on \({\mathbb{CP}}^1\) via the projection \(P\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda} \to P/B { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathbb{P}}^1\).

A trick: recovering \({\mathsf{K}}^G\) from \({\mathsf{K}}^T\) and the Weyl group action on it. This is why we reduce to \({\mathsf{K}}^T\) so often! Write \({\mathsf{K}}^G({\operatorname{pt}}) = R(G)\) on one hand and \(A(T)^W\) on the other (taking Weyl group invariants), define a map \([V] \mapsto \sum_{\lambda \in X(T)} n_\lambda e^{\lambda}\). Writing \(W = X^T \subseteq X = G/B\), we can use something due Bill Graham. It’s a fact that \(i^* {\mathsf{K}}_T(X) \to {\mathsf{K}}_T(X^T)\) is injective, and Bill shows \(i^*\) is an isomorphism after inverting certain elements.

The composite \(i^*i_* {\mathsf{K}}_T(X^T) \to {\mathsf{K}}_T(X^T)\) is multiplication by \(\lambda_T\), so here \(\lambda_{-1}\). Moreover \begin{align*} \lambda_T = \sum (-1)^i \Lambda^i N {}^{ \vee }\in {\mathsf{K}}_T(X_T) \end{align*} where \(N {}^{ \vee }\) is the conormal.

For \(X = {\mathbb{P}}^1\) and \(W = \left\{{1, s}\right\}\), we have

A formula due to Bill, there is an element: \begin{align*} {\mathsf{K}}_T(X) \ni \alpha = \sum_{w\in X^T} (i_w)_* \qty{ (i_w)^* \alpha \over \lambda_{-1} (N {}^{ \vee }_w)} .\end{align*}

For \([P\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} \in {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda}]\), we can compute \begin{align*} \pi_*[ P\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{ \lambda}] &= \pi_* \sum_{1, s} (i_w)_* \qty{ (i_w)^* [P\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{ \lambda}] \over \lambda_{-1} (N_w {}^{ \vee }) } \\ &= \pi_* \qty{ (i_1)_* \qty{ [B\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{ \lambda}] \over 1 - e^{\alpha}} + (i_s)_* \qty{ [sB\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{ \lambda}] \over 1 - e^{-\alpha}} }\\ &= \pi_* \qty{ (i_1)_* \qty{ e^{ \lambda} \over 1- e^{ \lambda}} + (i_s)_* \qty{ e^{ s\lambda} \over 1- e^{ \lambda}} }\\ &= \qty{ e^{ \lambda} \over 1- e^{ \lambda}} + \qty{ e^{ s\lambda} \over 1- e^{ \lambda}} \in A(T) .\end{align*}

\begin{align*} \pi_* [P\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda}] = {e^{\lambda} - s^{s \lambda + \alpha} \over 1 - e^{ \alpha}} .\end{align*}

Let \(q = e^{\alpha}\) and \(k \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={\left\langle {\lambda},~{ \alpha {}^{ \vee }} \right\rangle}\). Note that \begin{align*} s \lambda- \lambda = \lambda- {\left\langle {\lambda},~{ \alpha {}^{ \vee }} \right\rangle} - \lambda = -{\left\langle {\lambda},~{\alpha {}^{ \vee }} \right\rangle} \alpha .\end{align*} Then \begin{align*} (e^{ \lambda} - e^{ s \lambda+ \alpha})( 1- e^{ \alpha}) = e^{\lambda}(1 - e^{ - \alpha}) + e^{s \lambda}(1 - e^{ \alpha}) ,\end{align*} and we can write the RHS as \begin{align*} e^{ \lambda}\qty{ 1 - e^{ s \lambda- \lambda+ \alpha} \over 1 - e^{- \alpha }} = e^{ \lambda}\qty{ 1 - q^{1-k} \over 1 - q} = e^{\lambda} c(q) \end{align*} where \begin{align*} c(q) &= \begin{cases} 1 + q + \cdots + q^{-k} & k\leq 0 \\ 0 & k=0 \\ -\qty{q^{1-k} + q^{2-k} + \cdots + q^{-1}}& k\geq 1. \end{cases}\\ \\ &= \begin{cases} e^{ \lambda} + e^{ \lambda+ \alpha} + \cdots + e^{s \lambda}& k\leq 0 \\ 0 & k=0 \\ -\qty{ e^{s \lambda+ \alpha} + e^{s \lambda+ 2 \alpha} + \cdots + e^{s \lambda + (k-1) \alpha} }& k\geq 1. \end{cases} .\end{align*}

By Kumar, \begin{align*} D_s(e^{ \lambda}) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={e ^{ \lambda} - e^{s \lambda- \alpha} \over 1 - e^{- \alpha}} ,\end{align*} where \(e^{ \lambda}\) corresponds to \({\mathcal{L}}( \lambda)\).

27 Equivariant \({\mathsf{K}}{\hbox{-}}\)theory of \(G/P\) (Monday, November 01)

We’ll stick to the finite-type case for today. Setup: let \(G\in {\mathsf{Alg}}{\mathsf{Grp}}_{/ {{\mathbb{C}}}}\) be connected, semisimple, simply connected, with \(T\leq G\) a maximal torus. Goal: describe \({\mathsf{K}}_T(G/P)\).

Note that \begin{align*} {\mathsf{K}}_G(G/B) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_G(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\operatorname{pt}}) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_B({\operatorname{pt}}) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_T({\operatorname{pt}}) ,\end{align*} which we sometimes write as \({\mathsf{K}}_T\) or \(A(T)\), the representation ring of \(T\). General pattern: for \({\mathsf{K}}_G({-})\), look at \({\mathsf{K}}_T({-})^W\) instead, using that \({\mathsf{K}}_G({\operatorname{pt}}) = {\mathsf{K}}_T({\operatorname{pt}})^W = A(T)^W\). Writing \(P = LU\supseteq T\) for \(P\) a parabolic and \(L\) a Levi, we have \begin{align*} {\mathsf{K}}_G(G/P) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_P({\operatorname{pt}}) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_L({\operatorname{pt}}) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_T({\operatorname{pt}})^{W_Y} { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}A(T)^{W_Y} .\end{align*}

Thus there is a chain of isomorphisms: \begin{align*} {\mathsf{K}}_T(G/P) &{ { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_B(G/P) && \text{doesn't see unipotent radical} \\ &{ { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_G(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} G/P) && \text{induction}\\ &{ { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_G(G/B \overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} G/P) && \text{trivialization for algebraic fiber bundles} \\ &{ { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}{\mathsf{K}}_G(G/B) \otimes_{{\mathsf{K}}_G({\operatorname{pt}})} {\mathsf{K}}_G(G/P) && \text{Kunneth} \\ &{ { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}A(T) \otimes_{A(T)^W} A(T)^{W_Y} .\end{align*} Note that \(A(T) = {\mathbb{Z}}[X(T)] = {\mathbb{Z}}{ {}^{ \scriptscriptstyle\times^{\ell} } }\) for some \(\ell\).

This formula may hold in more generality, but we’re sticking with what’s in the literature for now.

Phrasing this in terms of equivariant line bundles: starting with \(\lambda\in X(T)\), we write it as \(e ^{\lambda} \in A(T)\), and we have two morphisms \(A(T) \to {\mathsf{K}}_T(G/B)\):

  1. \(F_1: e^{ \lambda} \to G/B \times {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda} \in {\mathsf{K}}_T(G/B)\).
  2. \(F_2: e^{\lambda} \to G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{ \lambda}\in {\mathsf{K}}_T(G/B)\).

Note that the latter can be projected onto \(G/B\). If \(e^{\lambda}\in R(G) = A(T)^W\), then \(G\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda} \cong G/B \times {\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda}\) since the \(B{\hbox{-}}\)action extends to a \(G{\hbox{-}}\)action. So these assemble to a map \begin{align*} F_1 \otimes F_2: A(T) \otimes_{A(T)^W} A(T) \to {\mathsf{K}}_T(G/B) .\end{align*} The claim is that this is equivalent to the isomorphism from above.

27.1 Equivariant Cohomology

Perhaps don’t try to learn this from Kumar as a first pass! See Anderson-Fulton for a good treatment. For fiber bundles, see Husemoller. For algebraic topology, see May’s “Concise Course..” chapter 18.

Studying the equivariant geometry of a space \(X\) is the same as studying fiber bundles with fiber \(X\).

Recalling some notions of axiomatic cellular cohomology: fix \(M\in {\mathsf{Ab}}{\mathsf{Grp}}\) and consider pairs \((X, A)\in {\mathsf{Top}}\). Then there exist functors \(H^k(X, A; M): {\mathsf{ho}}{\mathsf{Top}}{ {}^{ \scriptscriptstyle\times^{2} } } \to {\mathsf{Ab}}{\mathsf{Grp}}\) with natural transformations \(\delta: H^k(A; M) \to H^{k+1}(X, A; M)\), where \(H^k(A; M)\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= H^k(A, \emptyset; M)\). These satisfy and are characterized by a set of 5 axioms, which we’ll omit. Note that these constructions will work for any space we run into in this setting.

If \(B \subseteq A \subseteq X\), show that there is a LES

Link to Diagram

Let \(G\in \operatorname{Lie}{\mathsf{Grp}}\) with \(G\curvearrowright X\in {\mathsf{Top}}\) acting on the left.4 Write \(E\in {\mathsf{Top}}\) for any contractible space with a free right \(G{\hbox{-}}\)action, then define the \(G{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant cohomology of \(X\) as \begin{align*} H_G^k(X) \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= H^k(E \overset{\scriptscriptstyle {G} }{\times} X) .\end{align*}

Some facts:

  • \(X \simeq E\times X\).
  • \(H_G^k(X)\) does not depend on the homotopy representative of \(E\)
  • \({\mathbf{B}}G \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= E/G\) is the classifying space of \(G\).
  • If \(\xi:X\to Y\) equivariant with respect to \(\phi:G\to H\), there is a map \(EG\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {G} }{\times} X\to EH\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {H} }{\times} Y\) which induces \(\xi^*: H_H^*(Y) \to H_G^*(X)\). In particular, \(X\to {\operatorname{pt}}\) always exists, which is why \(H^*({\mathbf{B}}G)\) plays a large role.
  • If \(G\supseteq H\) and \(EG\) is given, then \(EH = EG\).

\begin{align*} H_G^*({\operatorname{pt}}) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}H^*(E\overset{\scriptscriptstyle {G} }{\times} {\operatorname{pt}}) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}H^*(E/G) { { \, \xrightarrow{\sim}\, }}H^*({\mathbf{B}}G) .\end{align*}

Examples of \({{\mathbf{B}}G}\):

  • For \(G = {\mathbb{C}}^n\), we have \({\mathsf{E} G}= G = {\mathbb{C}}^n\) and \(H_G^*({\operatorname{pt}}) = H^*({\operatorname{pt}})= M\).
  • For \(G = {\mathbb{C}}^{\times}\), \(E = {\mathbb{C}}^\infty\setminus\left\{{0}\right\}\) which is a contractible Ind-variety, and \({{\mathbf{B}}G}= {\mathsf{E} G}/G = {\mathbb{P}}^\infty_{/ {{\mathbb{C}}}}\).

28 Chern Classes and Intersection Theory (Wednesday, November 03)

28.1 Chern Classes

See Eisenbud and Harris, 3264 and All That, and Fulton.

Let \(G \in {\mathsf{Alg}}{\mathsf{Grp}}\) act transitively on \(X\) over \(k = { \mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5muk\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu }\) with \(\operatorname{ch}k = 0\) and let \(Y \leq X\) be a subvariety.

  1. If \(Z\leq X\) is a subvariety then there is an open dense subset of group elements \(U \subseteq G\) such that \(gZ \pitchfork Y\) generically.

  2. If \(\phi: Z\to X\) is a morphism of varieties, then for a generic \(g\in G\), the preimage \(\phi^{-1}(gY)\) is generally reduced and is of the same codimension as \(Y\).

  3. If \(G\) is affine then \([gY] = [Y]\) in the Chow group \(A(X)\).

See ELC article, a consequence is Bertini’s theorem.

Suppose \({\mathcal{E}}\in { {\mathsf{Bun}}\qty{\operatorname{GL}_{r}} }_{/ {Y}}\) and let \(1\leq i\leq r\). Let \(\sigma_0, \cdots, \sigma_{r-i}\) be global sections of \({\mathcal{E}}\) and \(Y_{\sigma} = Y( \sigma_0 \vee\cdots \vee\sigma_{r-i})\) be the degeneracy locus where they are linearly dependent, so \(\sigma_0 \vee\cdots \vee\sigma_{r-i}\) are sections of \(\bigwedge\nolimits^{r-i+1} {\mathcal{E}}\to Y\). Then

  1. No component of \(Y_{ \sigma}\) has codimension greater than \(i\),

  2. If the \(\sigma_i\) are general elements of \({\mathsf{{\mathbb{C}}}{\hbox{-}}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \(V \subseteq H^0({\mathcal{E}})\) be a subset of global sections generating \({\mathcal{E}}\), then \(Y_{ \sigma}\) is generically reduced with codimension \(i\) in \(Y\).

For affine \(Y\), locally thinking of functions, either \(f\) hits or misses completely any given irreducible component.

Let \(V\in{\mathsf{{\mathbb{C}}}{\hbox{-}}\mathsf{Mod}}\) with \(\dim_{\mathbb{C}}V = m\) be the module of global sections \(\sigma_0, \cdots, \sigma_{m-1}\) generating \({\mathcal{E}}\), and let \(\phi:Y\to {\operatorname{Gr}}_{m-r}(V)\) be given by \(y \mapsto \ker(V\to {\mathcal{E}}_y)\). If \(W \leq V\) is a submodule of dimension \(r-i+1\) spanned by \(\sigma_0, \cdots, \sigma_{r-i}\), then the locus \(Y_{ \sigma} \subseteq Y\) is the preimage \(\phi^{-1}(X_{\lambda}(W))\).

We can write \(X = {\operatorname{Gr}}_{m-r}(V) = G/P\) for \(G = \operatorname{GL}(V)\) to realize it as a projective homogeneous variety. Then \(X_{\lambda}(W) = \left\{{E \in {\operatorname{Gr}}_{m-r}(V) {~\mathrel{\Big\vert}~}\dim(W \cap E ) \geq 1}\right\}\) is a Schubert variety for any subspace \(0 \leq W \leq V\). In Young diagrams for a partition \(\lambda\), this condition corresponds to a valley:

There is a unique way of assigning to each vector bundle \({\mathcal{E}}\) on a \(X\) (assumed smooth) a class \(c({\mathcal{E}}) = 1 + c_1({\mathcal{E}}) + c_2({\mathcal{E}}) + \cdots \in A(X)\), noting that smooth \(X\) guarantees a ring structure on the Chow group. These satisfy

  1. (Line bundles): If \({\mathcal{L}}\to X\) is a line bundle then \(c({\mathcal{L}}) = 1 + c_1({\mathcal{L}})\) where \(c_1({\mathcal{L}}) \in A^1(X)\) is the class of the divisor of zeros minus the divisor of poles of any rational section of \({\mathcal{L}}\), defined up to rational equivalence in \(A(X)\).

  2. (Degeneracy locus): If \(\sigma_0, \cdots, \sigma_{r-i}\) are global sections of \({\mathcal{E}}\) and the degeneracy/dependence locus \(Y_{ \sigma} \subseteq X\) has codimension \(i\), then \(c_i({\mathcal{E}}) = [X_{ \sigma} ] \in A^i(X)\)

  3. (Whitney’s formula): If \(0 \to {\mathcal{E}}\to {\mathcal{F}}\to {\mathcal{G}}\to 0\) is a SES in \({ {\mathsf{Bun}}\qty{\operatorname{GL}_r} }_{/ {X}}\), then \(c({\mathcal{F}}) = c({\mathcal{E}})c({\mathcal{G}}) \in A(X)\).

  4. (Functoriality/compatibility with pullback): If \(\phi:X\to Y\) then \(\phi^*(c({\mathcal{E}})) = c(\phi^*({\mathcal{E}}))\).

This induces a map \(c: {\mathsf{K}}(X) \to A(X)\). Note that you can compose this with the cycle class map \(A(X)\to H^*_{{\mathrm{sing}}}(X)\).

We can define a total Chern class \(c({\mathcal{E}}) = \sum_i c_i({\mathcal{E}}) u^i \in R[u]\) for \(R\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= H^*_{{\mathrm{sing}}}(X)\).

Setup: take \(X\) paracompact and Hausdorff/T2, which will be necessary for partitions of unity. For \({\mathcal{E}}\xrightarrow{\pi} X \in { {\mathsf{Bun}}\qty{\operatorname{GL}_r} }({\mathbb{C}})_{/ {X}}\), there exist \(c_i({\mathcal{E}})\in H^{2i}(X)\) satisfying

  1. If \(f:X\to Y \in {\mathsf{Top}}\) then \(f^*(c_i({\mathcal{E}})) = c_i(f^* {\mathcal{E}})\).

  2. \(c_i({\mathcal{E}}) = 0\) unless \(o\leq i \leq r\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=\operatorname{rank}({\mathcal{E}})\), and \(c_0({\mathcal{E}}) = 1\)

  3. Exact sequences of vector bundles yield Whitney’s formula.

If additionally \(X\) is smooth,

  1. If \({\mathcal{L}}, {\mathcal{M}}\) are line bundles, then \(c_1({\mathcal{L}}\otimes{\mathcal{M}}) = c_1({\mathcal{L}}) + c_1({\mathcal{M}})\).

  2. If \(s:X\to {\mathcal{L}}\) is a nonzero section, writing \(Z(s) \subseteq X\) for its zero set, \([Z(s)] = c_1({\mathcal{L}}) \in H^2(X)\).

  3. For the projectivization \(\pi: {\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{E}})\to X\), there is a Poincaré duality: considering \({\mathcal{O}}(-1) \subseteq \pi^* {\mathcal{E}}\) and its dual \({\mathcal{O}}(1)\), \begin{align*} H^*({\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{E}})) = H^*(X)[\zeta] / \left\langle{ \zeta^r - c_1({\mathcal{E}} {}^{ \vee })\zeta^{r-1} + \cdots + (-1)^r c_r({\mathcal{E}} {}^{ \vee }) }\right\rangle .\end{align*}

For \(\operatorname{rank}A = 2\), we have \(\dim {\mathfrak{h}}= 3+1=4\). Up to a change of coordinates, we can use \(\alpha_1 {}^{ \vee }= {\left[ {1,0} \right]}^t\) and \(\alpha_2 {}^{ \vee }= {\left[ {1,0} \right]}^t\) and let \(V \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= R \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\left\{{\alpha_1 {}^{ \vee }, \alpha_2 {}^{ \vee }}\right\}\) be the ambient Euclidean space and set \(L\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={\mathbb{Z}}\left\langle{ \alpha_1, \alpha_2}\right\rangle\). Then use the action of \(W\) to define \(W_{\text{aff}} \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= L \rtimes W_f\) where \(W_f = W(A {}^{ \vee })\), and \(s_i(\chi) = \chi - {\left\langle { \alpha, \lambda},~{\alpha} \right\rangle} {}^{ \vee }\). Here we think of \(L\) as translations. The dual roots are \(\alpha_1 = {\left[ {2, -1} \right]}^t. \alpha_2 = {\left[ {-1, 2} \right]}\) and so \(\tilde \alpha = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 = {\left[ {1,1} \right]}^t\) Define hyperplanes \(H_{\alpha, n} \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=\left\{{v\in V {~\mathrel{\Big\vert}~}{\left\langle {\alpha},~{v} \right\rangle} = n \in {\mathbb{Z}}}\right\}\). There is a fundamental alcove enclosed by the positive sides of the various hyperplanes and within distance 1 of \(H_{\tilde \alpha, 0}\). If you draw the picture and now act on the fundamental alcove by simple reflections, the image “spirals” out away from the origin.

The article doesn’t use BSDH resolutions, maybe compare and contrast with what we’ve done.

Back to \(\mu\). For \(\ell = 1\), we have \begin{align*} P_1 \overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} P_2 \overset{\scriptscriptstyle {B} }{\times} P_3/B \xrightarrow{\mu} X_w .\end{align*}

The Bruhat order yields

Link to Diagram

Note that there are no braid relations. We can consider the \(T{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant multiplicity \({\mathcal{E}}_x^T X_w = \sum_{z\in \mu^{-1}(x)^T} {\mathcal{E}}_z^T(z)\) given by summing over the \(T{\hbox{-}}\)equivariant fixed points in the fiber. Here this just equals \({\mathcal{E}}_z^T(z)\) where \(\mu(z) = x\), since there is a unique \(T{\hbox{-}}\)fixed point in the fiber. A basic AG argument shows that the resolution is an isomorphism and thus \(X_w\) is smooth, so there is no singular locus. The paper gives a nice formula for \(\ell \geq 6\).

Starting the calculation:

  1. Consider \(e_x X_w\in \operatorname{ff}(S({\mathfrak{h}} {}^{ \vee }))\) the equivariant multiplicity, then \(x\in X_w\) is smooth iff a certain change of basis \(c_{w, x}\) corresponds to the equivariant multiplicity.
  2. In the rationally smooth locus, they show smoothness iff there is a single \(T{\hbox{-}}\)fixed point in the fiber.

33 Sasha’s Talk (Monday, November 29)

Topic: Segal-Sagawara construction. Define \(\mathrm{Witt} = \operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{Diff}^+ S^1)\), regarded as polynomial vector fields on \(S^1\). \(H^2(\mathrm{Witt}; {\mathbb{C}}) = {\mathbb{C}}\), so there is a 1-dimensional space of central extensions, with a distinguished one: the Virasoro algebra. There is a SES \(0 \to{\mathbb{C}}\mathrm{charge} \to \mathrm{Vir} \to \mathrm{Witt}\to 0\), and for \(LG\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= C^\infty(S^1, G)\), a SES \(0\to S^1 \to \tilde{LG} \to LG\to 0\). Here \(\mathrm{charge}\) is some distinguished central element. Does the Virasoro group act on this extension? Not quite, but almost – pass to Lie algebras to get \(0\to {\mathbb{C}}\to \tilde{L{\mathfrak{g}}}\to {\mathfrak{g}}\to 0\). Theorem: for \(\rho: \tilde{L{\mathfrak{g}}} \to \mathop{\mathrm{End}}_{\mathbb{C}}(V)\) an admissible representation, there is a representation \(\rho': \mathrm{Vir}\to \mathop{\mathrm{End}}_{\mathbb{C}}(V)\). Note \(L{\mathfrak{g}}\mathrel{\vcenter{:}}={\mathfrak{g}}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{C}}[t, t^{-1}]\). Write \(X_i \left\langle{m}\right\rangle \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}= X_i\otimes m\).

Admissible representations: for all \(v\in V\) and \(X\in{\mathfrak{g}}\), there exists an \(m\) such that \(\rho(X\left\langle{m}\right\rangle)(v) = 0\). Define the Casimir element \(\sum_i X_i X^i \in Z({\mathcal{U}}({\mathfrak{g}}))\). Levels: level \(\ell\) if \(\mathrm{charge}\) acts by \(\ell \cdot \operatorname{id}\). Critical level: \(\ell \neq \cdots\) some constant (roughly the dual Coxeter number), avoid this \(\ell\) for the reps in the theorem statement.
